claims.text: Cooling rate can alter the phase composition of high-entropy alloys.
The phase diversity in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during cooling and later thermal exposure originates from cooling-rate-dependent modulation of the nucleation barrier.
Rapid quenching maintains localized compositional fluctuations in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Rapid cooling produces greater undercooling than slow cooling.
Retained compositional fluctuations and undercooling lower the nucleation barrier for metastable phases.
Rapid cooling favors metastable or other non-equilibrium phases relative to slow cooling.
Rapid cooling may promote amorphous constituents.
Slow cooling provides enough atomic mobility for homogenization.
Slow cooling favors nucleation of equilibrium phases and produces a phase distribution closer to equilibrium predictions.
After identical isothermal exposures, rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will contain a higher fraction of metastable or non-equilibrium phases than the slow-cooled baseline.

The controlled comparison starts both Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 sample sets from the same high-temperature BCC state, slow-cools one set, rapidly quenches the other, and then applies identical isothermal exposures.
The relevant isothermal transformation window for Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is approximately 1100–1350 °C.
The cooling-rate effect should apply when undercooling is sufficient to retain local compositional heterogeneity.
The effect may not apply when the cooling-rate difference is too small to bypass compositional homogenization.
Long thermal exposures may erase the microstructural distinctions created by different cooling rates.
XRD, SEM, and TEM can be used to compare phase fractions, compositional fluctuations, amorphous regions, grain sizes, and phase-boundary distributions between the two cooling conditions.

Failure of rapidly quenched samples to show a statistically significant increase in metastable or non-equilibrium phase fraction relative to the slow-cooled samples would falsify the proposed cooling-rate mechanism.
